But as his anointing teaches you about everything. Key words. “Teaches” (didaskei). The Spirit teaches believers, guiding them into the truth (John 14:26; 16:13), not by giving new revelation, but by illuminating the apostolic word, confirming it in their hearts, and enabling them to discern error.

And is true, and is no lie. Key words. The Spirit is the Spirit of truth (John 14:17).

Just as it has taught you, abide in him. Key words. “Abide in him”: in Christ. The Spirit’s teaching always leads to Christ.

Where Christians differ: does this verse mean believers do not need teachers? Some have used this verse to reject all church teaching, or to claim private revelations from the Spirit. Verdict: John himself is teaching them in this very letter. Christ gave teachers to the church (Ephesians 4:11; 2 Timothy 2:2). John means they do not need the false teachers’ new “knowledge,” because the Spirit has given them the true knowledge through the apostolic gospel. The Spirit does not give new revelation that contradicts or adds to Scripture; he illuminates Scripture and confirms its truth to the heart. Every claim to Spirit-given teaching must be tested by the apostolic word (4:1–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should be independent of the church or of faithful teachers. It means they are not dependent on human teachers in the way the false teachers claimed, as if the Spirit were not enough.

In a sentence. As for you, the anointing you received from him remains in you, and you do not need anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about all things, and as that anointing is real, not counterfeit, just as it has taught you, remain in him.

For worship. Thank God for the Spirit who teaches you through his word. Ask him to illuminate Scripture as you read it today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–29 — Abide in Him: The Returning King and the Family Likeness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by looking to Christ’s return. John urges his dear children to remain in Christ now, so that when he appears they will meet him with confidence instead of shrinking from him in shame at his coming. Then he introduces a theme that will run through the rest of the letter: because God is righteous, everyone who practises righteousness shows the family likeness of one who has been born of him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Abide in him

Abide in Christ so as to have confidence at his coming. Those born of the righteous God practise righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Christ’s appearing was still ahead.

Now: Live now as someone who will meet him face to face.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.

And now, little children, abide in him. Key words. “Abide” (menete, keep remaining). The command that sums up the chapter.

So that when he appears. Key words. “Appears” (phanerōthē, is revealed, made visible). Christ’s second coming, visible and public.

We may have confidence. Key words. “Confidence” (parrēsian, boldness, freedom of speech, openness). Like a child running to greet a returning father, not hiding.

And not shrink from him in shame at his coming. Key words. “Shrink in shame” (aischynthōmen, be put to shame, shrink back ashamed). Those who have not abided in him will be ashamed. “Coming” (parousia, arrival, presence): the only use of this word in John’s writings.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be condemned if they are not perfect. It means those who abide in Christ will meet him with joyful confidence, not guilty fear.

In a sentence. And now, dear children, continue in him, so that when he appears we may be confident and unashamed before him at his coming.

For worship. Abide in Christ today, so that you can look forward to his coming with confidence and joy.

verseByVerse.quote: If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.

If you know that he is righteous. Key words. “He”: Christ (v. 1) or God the Father (since “born of him” refers to the Father). “Righteous” (dikaios).

You may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him. Key words. “Practices righteousness” (poiōn tēn dikaiosynēn, does righteousness, present tense: habitually). “Has been born of him” (ex autou gegennētai, perfect tense: has been begotten and remains so). The first mention of new birth in 1 John. Note the order: being born of God comes first; practising righteousness follows as the evidence. Not that doing right causes new birth, but that new birth produces doing right. Children resemble their Father. This is the test of righteousness, introducing chapter 3.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only the perfectly righteous are born again. It means a settled pattern of righteous living shows that one is God’s child.

In a sentence. If you know that he is righteous, you know that everyone who does what is right has been born of him.

For worship. Thank God for giving you new birth. Ask him to make you more like your Father in righteousness.

2.theology:
Advocacy and Propitiation. The paired terms of 2:1–2 give us the two aspects of Christ's saving work seen from different angles. As advocate, he represents us before the Father — our case is in his hands, and he is qualified to plead it because he is righteous. As propitiation, he has already dealt with the ground of the accusation — the wrath of God against our sin has been absorbed at the cross. These are not two separate acts but two perspectives on the one act of the cross. The same sacrifice that satisfied divine justice now grounds our ongoing access to divine mercy. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is both objective (propitiation — something accomplished outside us, in history, on a cross) and applied (advocacy — an ongoing ministry of Christ on our behalf). Both are necessary; together they produce the settled assurance John wants his readers to have.

The Three Tests. John's three tests — obedience (2:3–6), love (2:9–11), and belief (2:22–23) — are not a checklist for earning assurance but symptoms of new birth. Just as a doctor looks for signs of life, John looks for the signs that genuine regeneration has occurred. These tests are not meant to produce anxiety but clarity: not "have I been good enough?" but "is there genuine fruit of the Spirit in my life?" The tests are cumulative and mutually reinforcing — genuine obedience produces love; genuine love flows from right belief; genuine belief manifests in how we treat the brothers and sisters.
2.examples:
Then: The antichrists who had left the community had claimed a superior knowledge of God. Their departure seemed, to some, like the enlightened ones leaving the unenlightened behind. John's response is pastoral and pointed: the ones who left proved by their leaving that they were never truly of the community (2:19). This is not cruelty but theology — genuine new birth produces perseverance. The ones who remained, confused and perhaps diminished, were the ones who had "the anointing from the Holy One" and knew the truth (2:20). The test of authenticity is not sophistication but faithfulness to the beginning.

Now: We live in a world of novelty — new spiritualities, new therapies, new paths to self-actualization. The church is perpetually tempted to trade the apostolic gospel for something more culturally current, more psychologically satisfying, more intellectually respectable. John's word is the same: let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. The gospel does not need to be updated; it needs to be inhabited. The depth we seek is not found by moving beyond the cross — it is found by going deeper into it.

3.title: Children of God, Love in Deed
3.text: <sup>1</sup>See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.<sup>2</sup>Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.<sup>3</sup>And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.<sup>4</sup>Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.<sup>5</sup>You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.<sup>6</sup>No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.<sup>7</sup>Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.<sup>8</sup>Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.<sup>9</sup>No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God’s seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.<sup>10</sup>By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.<sup>11</sup>For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.<sup>12</sup>We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous.<sup>13</sup>Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.<sup>14</sup>We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.<sup>15</sup>Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.<sup>16</sup>By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.<sup>17</sup>But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?<sup>18</sup>Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.<sup>19</sup>By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him;<sup>20</sup>for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.<sup>21</sup>Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;<sup>22</sup>and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.<sup>23</sup>And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.<sup>24</sup>Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens in wonder: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are.” We are God’s children now, and when Christ appears we shall be like him. That hope makes us pure.

Then John shows what God’s children look like. They do not live in sin, because God’s seed abides in them and the Son came to destroy the devil’s works. And they love one another, not in words only, but in deeds, as Christ laid down his life for us. When the heart condemns, God is greater than our heart. His command is to believe in his Son and love one another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Children of God: Now and Not Yet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John commands us to look: “See what kind of love”. The phrase suggests something foreign and astonishing. God calls us his children, “and so we are”. The world does not recognise us, because it did not recognise him. We are children now; what we will be is not yet seen. But when Christ appears we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. And everyone with that hope purifies himself now.
verseByVerse.theology:
Children Now, Like Him Then

We are God’s children now; when Christ appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. That hope purifies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Some claimed they had already arrived.

Now: We become what we behold; set your hope on his appearing.

verseByVerse.quote: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See the astonishing love of the Father, who calls us his children, and so we are.

What kind of love. The word (potapēn) was used by the disciples of the man whom wind and sea obeyed (Matthew 8:27). This love comes from outside our world.

“And so we are.” Not a courtesy title, but a fact. The holy God has adopted rebels into his family.

On a Tuesday. You fail at work, or feel invisible at a party, or are laughed at for your faith. Before anything else, remember what you are: a child of the Father, loved with a love from another world. Let that move you to worship before it moves you to anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are God’s children now, and when Christ appears we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is.

Now and not yet. We are already children; the full glory of it is still hidden.

Seeing makes us like him. The vision of Christ produces the likeness. What a lifetime of sanctification has been moving towards, seeing him will complete in a moment.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This hope makes believers purify themselves as Christ is pure.

Hope that works. Real hope in Christ’s return pulls the future into the present. The standard is his own purity.

What it does not mean. It is not achieved sinlessness, which 1:8 rules out. It is the direction of a life that is being shaped towards the one it hopes to see.

On a Tuesday. A bride getting ready for her wedding does not need to be told to take care of her dress. Hope shapes behaviour. So does the hope of meeting Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Sin, the Devil, and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This passage must be read carefully, or it will either terrify the true believer or comfort the false one. John speaks of two families, known by how they live. The devil has sinned from the beginning; the Son of God appeared to destroy his works. God’s seed abides in those born of him, so that sin is no longer the settled pattern of their lives. John is not teaching sinless perfection (1:8–10), but that the new birth changes the direction of a life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The New Birth

The Son appeared to take away sins and to destroy the works of the devil. God’s seed abides in those born of him, so that sin is no longer the settled pattern of their lives.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Claimed spiritual knowledge was being used to excuse sin.

Now: Avoid both errors: tolerating sin as normal, and thinking that any sin proves you are not born again.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin is lawlessness.

What sin is. At heart, sin is rebellion against God’s authority, not just breaking social rules or a psychological problem. Every sin, however small, shares in that rebellion.

verseByVerse.quote: You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ appeared to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.

Why he came. The cross was not an afterthought; it was the mission. “Take away” means to lift and carry off (John 1:29).

Sinless. Only the one with no sin could bear the sins of others. Christ’s sinlessness is the foundation of the atonement.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who abides in Christ keeps on sinning.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a true Christian never sins. John has just said that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself (1:8), and he has given the remedy for sin (2:1). He means a settled, unrepentant pattern of sin.

A note on grammar. The ESV’s “keeps on sinning” reflects the Greek present tense. But tense alone does not prove a habit; that is a common exegetical fallacy. What makes it clear is the context: John has already told believers they will sin and must confess. The contrast is between a life that fights sin and a life at peace with it.

On a Tuesday. A believer who has fallen again into the same sin wonders whether she was ever a Christian. Her grief over it, and her running back to Christ, are signs of new life. The person John warns about is the one who sins and no longer cares.
verseByVerse.note: The verbs point to a settled habit of sin, not a single lapse (compare 1:8–2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever practises righteousness is righteous, as Christ is.

Evidence, not cause. We do not become righteous by doing right; we do right because God has made us righteous in Christ. But that gift always shows itself. The false teachers offered a spirituality without a matching life. John will not allow the split.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil.

Two families. A life given over to sin bears the family likeness of the devil.

Destroy. The verb means to undo, dismantle, loosen. Christ entered the territory the devil thought he owned and began taking his works apart: sin’s power, death’s reign, the accuser’s hold. The outcome is not in doubt.

On a Tuesday. A habit has held you for years and you feel it will never break. The Son of God appeared to destroy precisely this kind of thing. Fight it in his strength, and praise him for every inch he wins.

verseByVerse.quote: No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God's seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those born of God do not keep on sinning, because God’s seed abides in them.

God’s seed. The new birth implants God’s own life, which goes on working. That life is at war with sin and pulls towards God.

“Cannot”. Not that the believer is unable to commit a sin, but that he cannot settle into sin as his way of life. Sin in a Christian is always out of place, resisted and confessed.

A wrong view. Some teach that believers can reach a state where they no longer sin. John’s own words exclude it (1:8, 10). Others treat sin in Christians as normal and harmless. John excludes that too.

verseByVerse.quote: By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s children are known by righteousness and love for their brothers.

No neutral ground. Behind every life is a spiritual parentage, revealed by its direction. The two signs, righteousness and love, belong together, and the next verses develop the second.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — Love One Another: The Cain Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John brings love down to earth: the brother in front of you. He starts with Cain, who hated and murdered his brother because Abel was righteous. That is why the world hates believers. Then comes the clearest definition of love in the New Testament: “By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us.” The cross defines love, and obliges us to love the same way, starting with an open hand to a brother in need.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love Defined by the Cross

Cain hated his brother; Christ laid down his life for us. By this we know love, and we ought to lay down our lives for one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The world’s hatred was not to surprise the church.

Now: Love in deed and truth: an open hand to a brother in need.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message from the beginning is that we should love one another.

Not advanced teaching. Love is not an optional extra for the mature. It is the apostolic message itself, and what the gospel produces in those who receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must not be like Cain, who murdered his brother because his own deeds were evil.

Why Cain killed. Abel’s righteousness exposed Cain’s evil. Goodness does not need to speak to accuse; its presence is enough. That is why the world often resents faithful believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers should not be surprised that the world hates them.

Expect it. Jesus said it would happen (John 15:18–19). It is not a sign that God is displeased or that you have failed. The right response is not retaliation, not compromise and not self-pity, but steady faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for the brothers shows that we have passed from death to life.

Evidence of life. Love for other Christians is not just a nice trait; it is a fingerprint of the new birth. We crossed from death to life, and the love that now marks us shows it.

On a Tuesday. You doubt your salvation. Ask: do I love God’s people? Do I want to be with them, help them, forgive them? If so, that love is evidence of the Spirit’s work. Thank God for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hatred is murder of the heart, and no murderer has eternal life.

Murder in the heart. John echoes Jesus (Matthew 5:21–22): hatred is murder at the root.

What it does not mean. It is not a threat against a believer who feels anger and fights it. It describes a life marked by settled, unrepented hatred.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.

The cross defines love. We do not bring our own idea of love to the cross. The cross teaches us what love is.

We owe it. “Ought” means we are in debt. The same verb John uses for Christ laying down his life is now applied to us.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s love cannot abide in someone who closes his heart to a brother in need.

The concrete test. Not martyrdom, which may never be asked, but the need you can see, with resources you have. “Closes his heart” pictures shutting off compassion on purpose.

On a Tuesday. A family in your church has lost an income. You hear about it and feel sorry for them. John asks what you will do. Love may look like a bag of shopping, a quiet gift, or an evening babysitting so they can rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love must be shown in deeds and truth, not only words.

Deed and truth. Kind words are not enough, and can deceive us into thinking we have loved. Real love does something, and does it sincerely, not for applause. John includes himself: “let us”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — Assurance, Prayer, and the Mutual Indwelling
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After such a demanding call to love, the question follows: what if I have not loved enough? What if my heart condemns me? John answers tenderly: God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything. Then comes the freedom of prayer, and a summary of the whole Christian life: believe in the name of God’s Son, and love one another. The Spirit he has given assures us that he lives in us.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Greater than Our Heart

When our heart condemns us, God is greater and knows everything. His commandment is to believe in his Son and to love one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Assurance rested on love in deed and on the Spirit given to them.

Now: A tender conscience can rest in God’s fuller knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Practical love reassures our hearts before God, who is greater than our hearts and knows everything.

Two readings. Some read “God is greater than our heart” as a warning: if our conscience condemns us, God, who knows even more, condemns us more. Most read it as comfort, and the context supports that: John is reassuring the heart. God’s knowledge of us is truer than our own. He sees faith beneath the failures and real love in imperfect deeds.

On a Tuesday. A sensitive believer lies awake, sure she has failed God beyond repair. Her heart condemns her. John tells her to look past her heart to God, who knows everything, including the blood of his Son and the love he has put in her. She can rest there.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
When our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God.

Boldness. The word (parrēsia) means open-faced freedom. A peaceful conscience is not proof of perfection, but a gift that frees us to approach God without cringing.

verseByVerse.quote: and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obedient children receive what they ask from God.

What it does not mean. It is not a transaction where obedience unlocks answers, nor a promise of anything we fancy. Those who live to please God increasingly ask for what pleases him, and he is glad to give it (5:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s command is to believe in the name of his Son and to love one another.

One command. John uses the singular. Faith and love are two sides of one response: real faith in Christ always produces love, and real Christian love is always rooted in faith in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever keeps God’s commands abides in God, and we know God abides in us by the Spirit he has given.

Mutual indwelling. The believer is in God, and God in the believer, the closest union there is (John 15:4).

The Spirit’s witness. We know this by the Spirit, who produces love, testifies that we are God’s children (Romans 8:16), and keeps us in the truth. Assurance rests finally not on our feelings, but on God’s gift.

3.theology:
Adoption and Transformation. The doctrine of adoption is one of the richest in the New Testament, and 3:1–3, with its language of being born of God and called his children, is one of its highest expressions. To be called children of God is not a metaphor of religious devotion; it is a declaration of a new ontological status. We have been brought into the family of God — not as servants, not as subjects, but as children who share in the inheritance of the Son. And adoption in John is both present reality ("so we are," v.1) and future consummation ("what we will be has not yet appeared," v.2). The "not yet" of our glorification does not undermine the "already" of our adoption; the hope of the appearing purifies the life of the one who holds it.

Love Defined by the Cross. John's definition of love in verse 16 is one of the most consequential sentences in the New Testament. He does not say "God is love, therefore love is whatever feels loving." He says love is defined by a specific act: the laying down of the life of the Son. The cross is love's definition, love's measure, and love's demand. Reformed theology has always insisted that the love of God is not sentimentality but holy self-giving at infinite cost. Every theology of love that avoids the cross will eventually become a theology of tolerance — and tolerance is not love. Love is the cross, and the cross makes demands.
3.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had experienced the pain of betrayal — people they had loved had left. The temptation in such a situation is to turn inward, to protect the heart, to love in word only and keep the real self safely guarded. John's word to them is the cross: he laid down his life. Not as an inspiration to imitate from a safe distance, but as the very definition and pattern of what love is. The ones who remained in the fellowship were called to love one another with an openness that made them vulnerable — precisely because that is what love, defined by the cross, requires.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that defines love primarily as acceptance and validation. John defines it as sacrifice. The question is not "do I feel warmly toward my brother?" but "am I laying anything down for my brother?" The test of love is not interior but behavioural — not word and talk but deed and truth. A closed hand toward a brother in need, whatever feelings accompany it, is not love in John's sense. The cross makes love costly, specific, and concrete.

4.title: Testing the Spirits and the Love of God
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.<sup>2</sup>By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God,<sup>3</sup>and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.<sup>4</sup>Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.<sup>5</sup>They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.<sup>6</sup>We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.<sup>8</sup>Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.<sup>9</sup>In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.<sup>10</sup>In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.<sup>11</sup>Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.<sup>12</sup>No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.<sup>13</sup>By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.<sup>14</sup>And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.<sup>15</sup>Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.<sup>16</sup>So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.<sup>17</sup>By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.<sup>18</sup>There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.<sup>19</sup>We love because he first loved us.<sup>20</sup>If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.<sup>21</sup>And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 begins with a warning and rises to the fullest teaching on the love of God in the New Testament. The warning: test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out. The test is whether a teaching confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

Then John says twice, “God is love” (vv. 8, 16). He never lets this become vague. God’s love is defined by its greatest act: he sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. That love casts out the fear of punishment, and it flows on through us to one another: “We love because he first loved us.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Testing the Spirits: Discernment in the Last Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits.” Not every teaching that claims to come from God does. False prophets rarely announce themselves; they use Christian words with spiritual intensity. John’s test goes to the heart of the gospel: does the teaching confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? And he ends with confidence: “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing the Spirits

Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: False prophets had gone out into the world.

Now: Ask of any teaching whether it confesses the whole Christ — truly God, truly man, crucified and risen.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must test the spirits, for many false prophets have gone into the world.

A duty for all. The command is to the whole church, not only its leaders. Discernment is every believer’s responsibility.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suspicion of everyone, or refusing to learn from teachers. It means weighing what we hear against the apostolic gospel, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11).

verseByVerse.quote: By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of God confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh; the spirit that denies him is antichrist.

The test. Does it confess the real incarnation, the eternal Son truly and permanently become man? A teaching that separates the divine Christ from the human Jesus, or treats his body as a costume, fails.

A textual note. In v. 3 a few early writers and the Latin Vulgate read “every spirit that dissolves (or divides) Jesus”. Almost all Greek manuscripts read “does not confess Jesus”, and that is very likely original. The variant, though, shows how early readers understood the error: dividing Jesus from the Christ.

On a Tuesday. A popular spiritual book says that “the Christ” is a universal consciousness that Jesus happened to discover. It sounds deep. John’s test is simple: is Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen, confessed as the Christ come in the flesh? If not, put the book down.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers have overcome the false prophets, for the one in them is greater than the one in the world.

Already overcome. John does not leave the church anxious. The victory has already happened. Its ground is not their cleverness but the one who lives in them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers cannot be deceived, or need not watch; John has just told them to test. It means they need not fear. The weakest believer carries a greater power than the spirit behind every false teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
False prophets speak the world’s language, and the world listens to them.

Popularity is no proof. They are shaped by what the world finds respectable and comforting, so the world welcomes them. When a message is warmly received by people who have no interest in Christ, it is worth testing all the more.

verseByVerse.quote: We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever knows God listens to the apostles: this is how truth and error are recognised.

The apostolic word. John speaks as an apostle. Those who know God recognise and receive the apostolic teaching, as sheep know their shepherd’s voice (John 10:4). Today that means receiving the New Testament as God’s word.

Two tests together. The content of the confession (vv. 2–3) and a Spirit-given recognition of the apostolic word go together. Neither stands alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — God Is Love: The Source, the Measure, and the Goal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “God is love.” John does not mean a warm feeling or a tolerant mood. Love is the life the Father, Son and Spirit have shared from eternity. And this love has been shown: God sent his only Son so that we might live through him, as the propitiation for our sins. Since God so loved us, we ought to love one another. And when we do, the invisible God is seen in his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Love

Love is from God, and God showed it by sending his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The departing teachers’ knowledge produced schism, not love.

Now: No one has ever seen God; when we love one another, his love is made complete in us.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must love one another, for love is from God.

Love from God. Christian love does not start in our natural kindness. It flows from God, and it shows that we have been born of him.

Doctrine and love. John moves straight from testing doctrine to love. They are not alternatives for different temperaments, but one life.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.

God is love. Not only that God is loving, but that love is what he is: the Father loving the Son and the Son the Father in the Spirit, before there was any world. To know such a God and remain unloving is impossible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there is no hell, or that God will condemn no one. John has also said, “God is light” (1:5). And he defines love by the cross: God “sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (v. 10). Propitiation means turning away wrath. God’s love does not cancel his justice; it satisfies it at infinite cost. Nor does it mean that “love is God”, so that every human love is divine. John defines love by God, not God by our ideas of love.

verseByVerse.quote: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God showed his love by sending his only Son so that we might live through him.

A real event. Love is not just an idea. It happened: God sent his only Son. “Only” (monogenēs) shows the cost: not one messenger among many, but the unique Son.

Life for the dead. Without Christ we are spiritually dead (Ephesians 2:1). God’s love comes down into our death and brings life.

verseByVerse.quote: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love is God’s love for us in sending his Son as the propitiation for our sins.

The direction of love. It runs from God to us. We did not start it. We were loved before we loved.

Propitiation. The Son bore the penalty God’s holiness required, so that sinners could be welcomed without justice being set aside.

On a Tuesday. On days when your love for God feels thin, do not start with your love. Start here: he loved you and sent his Son. Your love will grow as you look at his.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since God so loved us, we must love one another.

Obligation and power. “If” means “since”. Those loved at such cost have no right to withhold love. And God’s love, poured into our hearts by the Spirit (Romans 5:5), is not only a model to copy but a power to draw on.

verseByVerse.quote: No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has seen God, but when we love one another, his love is perfected in us.

God seen in his people. The invisible God becomes visible when his people love each other across every difference. His love reaches its goal when it flows through us to others.

On a Tuesday. A church where wealthy and poor, old and young, sit together, eat together and care for one another shows the world something no argument can. Your small act of love this week is part of that picture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Abiding in Love: Confidence, Fear Cast Out, and the Visible Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Assurance rests on the Spirit God has given (v. 13) and the confession of his Son (v. 15). From that union comes confidence even for the day of judgment, because “as he is so also are we in this world.” Perfect love casts out the fear of punishment. And love for the invisible God is tested by love for the brother we can see.
verseByVerse.theology:
Fear Cast Out

Those who abide in love have confidence for the day of judgement. Perfect love casts out fear, and we love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Confidence rested on union with the Son, not on claimed knowledge.

Now: The brother we can see tests our love for the God we cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gift of the Spirit assures us that we abide in God and he in us.

The Spirit’s witness. We do not deduce our union with God from our achievements or feelings. God has given us his Spirit, who testifies that we are his children (Romans 8:16), produces love and keeps us confessing Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles testify that the Father sent the Son as Saviour of the world.

Eyewitnesses. John again rests his message on what was seen.

What it does not mean. “Saviour of the world” does not mean that every person will be saved. It means that Christ is not a tribal or national saviour, but the only Saviour for people of every nation, and fully able to save all who come to him (John 4:42).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God abides in God.

Confession. Confessing Jesus as God’s Son is not a work that earns union with God. It is the open hand of faith that receives it.

verseByVerse.quote: So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God.

Know and believe. Both: understanding God’s love and trusting it.

Living in love. Love is not something we add to our relationship with God. It is the atmosphere in which God dwells. Where real, Christ-shaped love is, God is.

verseByVerse.quote: By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love made complete gives confidence for the day of judgment.

Confidence for judgment day. The ground is not our moral record but our union with Christ. “As he is”, not as he was: the risen, vindicated Son, in whom we are hidden (Colossians 3:3). The judgment we deserved, he bore. His verdict, “beloved Son”, is shared with those in him.

verseByVerse.quote: There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Perfect love casts out the fear of punishment.

Which fear? The fear of punishment: the dread of a slave who expects a beating.

What it does not mean. It does not abolish the fear of the Lord. Scripture calls believers to reverent awe before God (Proverbs 1:7; Hebrews 12:28–29; 1 Peter 1:17). That holy fear is not the opposite of love but its companion. The more we grasp God’s love at the cross, the more we tremble at his holiness, and the less we fear his condemnation.

On a Tuesday. A believer who still lives in dread of God’s anger does not need to try harder. He needs to look longer at the cross, where the punishment was borne. Then he will fear God as a child reveres a holy Father, not as a criminal fears a judge.

verseByVerse.quote: We love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We love because God first loved us.

The whole gospel in brief. God’s love came first; ours is the response. We do not love in order to be loved, but because we are already loved.

A textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “We love him”. The earlier and better manuscripts simply read “We love”. The shorter reading is more likely original, and it is broader: God’s love produces our love for him and for others.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever claims to love the unseen God while hating a visible brother is a liar.

The visible test. It is easy to claim love for an invisible God. The test is the actual person in front of you, with all their faults.

On a Tuesday. You love worship on Sunday but avoid the member who annoys you. John says the two cannot be separated. Pray for that person by name, and look for one way to do them good this week.

verseByVerse.quote: And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands that whoever loves him must love his brother also.

One command. Love for God and love for his children are not two duties to balance, but one obedience. The chapter began with testing the spirits and ends with love: the Spirit of truth always produces love, and the spirit of error, sooner or later, produces division.

4.theology:
God is Love. The statement "God is love" (vv. 8, 16) is one of the most misused sentences in Scripture. It is taken to mean that love is God — that whatever we call love must be divine, that God must approve of whatever we name as love. John means the opposite: God defines love, not the other way around. And he defines it immediately by a specific act: the sending of the Son to be the propitiation. To say "God is love" in John's sense is to say that God, in his innermost being, is the kind of God who sends his only Son into the world to die for sinners who could not save themselves. That is the love John is talking about. It is not soft; it is costly. It is not tolerant; it is propitiatory. It is not vague; it has flesh and blood and a cross and an empty tomb.

The Expulsion of Fear. The pastoral application of the doctrine of propitiation in verses 17–18 is one of the most comforting passages in the New Testament. The believer who is tortured by fear of God's judgment has not yet fully grasped what the propitiation means: that the very wrath they fear has been exhausted, absorbed, satisfied in the beloved Son. Perfect love casts out fear not by denying the reality of judgment but by pointing to the one who bore it. Reformed theology speaks of the "double jeopardy" of the cross: it would be unjust for God to punish twice what Christ has already borne. The blood of Jesus is the answer to every accusing conscience, every fear of condemnation, every midnight terror of a soul that wonders whether it is safe with God.
4.examples:
Then: The community had been shaken by teachers who claimed spiritual authority and offered a more sophisticated understanding of God. The test John gives is arrestingly simple: do they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? Not "do they seem spiritual?" Not "do they have impressive experiences?" But: do they hold to the incarnation? This is always the fault line. Every theological error that has ever devastated a church has at some point compromised either the full deity or the full humanity of Christ. John's readers are given a test simple enough for a child and decisive enough to unmask every false spirit.

Now: "We love because he first loved us" is the answer to every form of Christian guilt and striving. The Christian life is not a performance of love in order to earn God's approval; it is a response of love to a love already given, already completed, already victorious at the cross. When love runs dry — as it will — the answer is not to try harder but to go back to the source: "In this is love, not that we have loved God..." The spring of all Christian love is the love of God in the cross of his Son. Drink there again, and love will flow.

5.title: Faith that Overcomes, Life that is Sure

And his commandments are not burdensome.<sup>4</sup>For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.<sup>5</sup>Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?<sup>6</sup>This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.<sup>7</sup>For there are three that testify:<sup>8</sup>the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.<sup>9</sup>If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.<sup>10</sup>Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.<sup>11</sup>And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.<sup>12</sup>Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.<sup>13</sup>I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.<sup>14</sup>And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.<sup>15</sup>And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.<sup>16</sup>If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that.<sup>17</sup>All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.<sup>18</sup>We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.<sup>19</sup>We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.<sup>20</sup>And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.<sup>21</sup>Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
5.overview:
The last chapter draws the letter’s threads together. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, loves God’s children and overcomes the world, and the victory is faith. God has testified about his Son, and his testimony is this: eternal life is in the Son. “Whoever has the Son has life.”

Then John states his purpose: “that you may know that you have eternal life.” Not hope or feel, but know. Those who know may pray with confidence and intercede for a sinning brother. The letter ends with Jesus Christ declared “the true God and eternal life”, and one last command: keep yourselves from idols.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Faith, Love, and the World-Overcoming Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John ties faith, new birth and love together as a single reality. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Messiah has been born of God, and anyone who loves the Father loves his children too. We know we love God’s children when we love God and keep his commands, and his commands are not a crushing weight. For everyone born of God overcomes the world, and the victory that overcomes the world is our faith. Who overcomes the world? Only the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as the Victory

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God and loves God’s children. Faith in the Son of God overcomes the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ordinary faith in Jesus was being called insufficient.

Now: The faith that overcomes is not heroic; it is trust in the Son of God who has already won.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and loves God’s other children.

Birth and faith. The Greek tense says the believer “has been born” of God. New birth is the source of faith, and faith is the evidence of new birth. This is a strong text for the Reformed teaching that regeneration comes before, and produces, faith (John 1:12–13).

Family love. If you love the Father, you will love his children. Love for the head of the family reaches the whole family.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know we love God’s children when we love God and keep his commands.

Two directions. In 4:20, love for the visible brother tested love for God. Here love for God tests love for the brother. They are not in tension. True love for others is shaped by obedience to God, and obedience to God includes loving others. Love that ignores God’s commands is not love for his children.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for God is keeping his commands, which are not burdensome.

Not burdensome. The word means heavy or crushing. For those born of God, his law is not an outside weight but the expression of a new heart that delights in his will (Psalm 119:35).

What it does not mean. It does not mean obedience is never hard. Christ called us to take up a cross. It means God’s commands are not a crushing yoke, because he gives the love and strength to keep them (Matthew 11:30).

On a Tuesday. If obeying God feels like nothing but a grind, the answer is not only to try harder. Ask whether you have stopped looking at his love. Return to the cross, and the commands will feel more like a path home than a weight.

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone born of God overcomes the world, and faith is the victory.

Already won. Christ said, “I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Faith is the hand that holds on to the one who has already won, and so shares his victory.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God overcomes the world.

Faith in this person. Not general spirituality or self-belief, but faith in Jesus as God’s Son. The question shuts out every other way, and opens the door to anyone who believes.

On a Tuesday. A young Christian at university feels outnumbered and outargued. She does not overcome the world by winning every debate, but by trusting the Son of God, who has already overcome it. That frees her to speak with courage and kindness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Three Witnesses and the Life That Is in the Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under Jewish law a matter was settled by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). God provides three: the Spirit, the water and the blood. The water and blood mark the beginning and end of Jesus’ ministry, his baptism and his death. God’s own testimony is greater than any human testimony, and it is this: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. There is no middle ground: whoever has the Son has life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Three Witnesses

The Spirit, the water and the blood agree: the one who was baptised is the one who died. God has given eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teaching separated the Christ of the baptism from the Jesus of the cross.

Now: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus Christ came by water and blood, his baptism and his death, and the Spirit testifies.

What water and blood mean. Some take them as the water and blood from Jesus’ side (John 19:34); others as baptism and the Lord’s Supper. The most likely reading is Jesus’ baptism, where his ministry began, and his death, where it was completed. The false teachers said the divine Christ came on Jesus at his baptism and left before the cross. John insists that the same Son of God was baptised and crucified: “not by the water only but by the water and the blood.”

Why it matters. If only a man died on the cross, there is no atonement. The Son of God himself shed his blood.
verseByVerse.note: “Water and blood” probably refer to Jesus’ baptism and his death — against teachers who said the divine Christ left Jesus before the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For there are three that testify: the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit, the water and the blood agree in their testimony.

Enough testimony. Three witnesses speak with one voice about Jesus. Those who deny him do not lack evidence.

A textual note. The King James Version adds words here about the Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost bearing witness in heaven, “and these three are one”. This addition, known as the Johannine Comma, is missing from almost every Greek manuscript before the sixteenth century and appears first in late Latin copies, apparently as a marginal comment. It is almost certainly not original. Nothing is lost: the Trinity is taught throughout Scripture and never depended on this line.
verseByVerse.note: Some late manuscripts add words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven (known from the King James Version). They are not in the early Greek manuscripts and the ESV omits them.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s testimony about his Son is greater than any human testimony.

From lesser to greater. We trust human witnesses every day, in courts, history books and doctors’ reports. God cannot lie. He has testified about his Son at his baptism (Matthew 3:17), by raising him from the dead (Romans 1:4) and by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To refuse God’s testimony is to make him a liar.

Inner witness. The Spirit confirms in the believer what the apostles proclaimed (Romans 8:16).

Unbelief is not neutral. To hear God’s clear testimony and refuse it is to call him a liar. Unbelief is not simply lack of information; it is a refusal to trust God.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s testimony is that he has given us eternal life in his Son.

A gift in a person. Eternal life is given, already, to be received. And it is found in the Son, not apart from him. No ritual or effort can give life outside Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life.

No middle ground. Life is not a matter of degrees here. The Son is either received by faith or not. This is the widest invitation (anyone may have the Son) and the narrowest claim (there is no other way to life).

On a Tuesday. A kind, moral neighbour says she has no need of Jesus. It feels harsh to say she lacks life. But love tells the truth gently, and offers the Son, in whom life is freely given.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Knowing What We Have in Christ: Assurance, Prayer, and the True God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John states his purpose: “that you may know that you have eternal life.” Those who know may pray boldly, intercede for a brother who sins, and rest in three great certainties: the one born of God is kept from the evil one; we belong to God while the world lies in the power of the evil one; and the Son of God has come and given us understanding to know the true God. He is “the true God and eternal life”. So keep yourselves from idols.
verseByVerse.theology:
That You May Know

John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life. They may pray with confidence, intercede for a sinning brother, and rest in what they know.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The letter closes on Jesus Christ as the true God and eternal life.

Now: Having the true God, refuse every substitute.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes so that believers may know that they have eternal life.

Know. Not hope, guess or feel on good days, but know. Assurance is not arrogance. It is the right response to the reliability of God’s word about his Son.

The tests and assurance. John’s tests of belief, obedience and love are not meant to make sincere believers anxious, but to give them certainty. They also expose false confidence.

On a Tuesday. A Christian is asked, “Are you sure you will go to heaven?” She hesitates, afraid of sounding proud. She can answer humbly, “Yes, not because I am good, but because God has given me life in his Son, and he does not lie.”
verseByVerse.note: John’s Gospel was written that readers might believe; this letter that believers might know they have eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We can be confident that God hears whatever we ask according to his will.

According to his will. This is not a limit that lowers expectations, but a promise: prayer that matches God’s will is always heard. It turns prayer from anxious pleading into confident alignment with what God is doing.

verseByVerse.quote: And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If he hears us, we have what we ask.

“We have”. Not “we will have”. God’s hearing is as good as his giving, even before we see the answer.

What it does not mean. It is not a blank cheque for any wish called prayer. It is the confidence of someone whose asking has been shaped by God’s will and word.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that. All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers should pray for a brother whose sin is not unto death.

What is the “sin leading to death”? Three main views. Some see the unforgivable sin of blasphemy against the Spirit (Matthew 12:31–32). Some see sin that brings physical death as God’s discipline, as with Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–11). The most likely view, in the context of this letter, is settled, unrepentant denial of Christ by those who have left the church (2:19, 22). We should not be dogmatic.

What it does not mean. John does not forbid prayer for anyone. He simply does not command it in that case. And he does not mean a Christian who has fallen badly is beyond hope; his main point is the opposite: pray, and God gives life.

On a Tuesday. You learn that a church friend has fallen into serious sin. The temptation is to gossip or to give up on him. John says: pray for him, by name, and go to him gently. God gives life through the prayers of his people.
verseByVerse.note: The “sin that leads to death” is probably the settled rejection of Christ shown by those who left the church.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those born of God do not keep on sinning, for the Son of God keeps them.

Who protects? “He who was born of God” is almost certainly Christ, the unique Son, who keeps his own (John 10:28; 17:12). Some manuscripts read “keeps himself”, but the reading the ESV follows, that Christ keeps him, fits the context and has strong support.

What it does not mean. It is not a promise of freedom from temptation or attack. It means the evil one cannot lay hold of the believer to destroy him. The Christian is not untouched by battle, but cannot be finally defeated.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We belong to God, while the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.

Two domains. The world “lies” in the evil one’s power, like someone asleep in an enemy’s arms, unaware. Believers live in hostile territory, but belong to God, kept by the one in them who is greater (4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of God has come and given us understanding to know the true God; he is the true God and eternal life.

The circle closes. The letter began with the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared (1:2). It ends by declaring that this life is Jesus Christ himself.

“He is the true God.” Some think “he” refers to the Father. But the nearest person named is Jesus Christ, and John has just called him “eternal life” (1:2; 5:11). This is one of the clearest statements of Christ’s deity in the New Testament.

For worship. The Christian does not merely know about God. Through the Son, we know him, and we are in him. That is the end of all theology: adoration.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, keep yourselves from idols.

An abrupt, fitting end. In Ephesus, real idols filled the streets. But an idol is anything that takes the place of the true God: a false picture of Christ, a love that rules the heart, a teacher who offers less than “the true God and eternal life”.

The best protection. Not anxious watchfulness alone, but deep delight in the one who is true. Those who treasure the real are less easily fooled by counterfeits.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you turn to when you are anxious, bored or hurt: your phone, food, work, someone’s approval. Name it, turn back to Christ, and tell him he is better.

5.theology:
Faith as Victory. The declaration of 5:4 — "this is the victory that has overcome the world — our faith" — is one of the most important statements about the nature of faith in Scripture. Faith is not a spiritual achievement, a heightened state of consciousness, or a moral virtue we cultivate. It is a hand that receives, a trust that rests, a confidence that looks away from itself to the Son of God who has already overcome. "Has overcome" — this points to the finished work of Christ at the cross as the source and ground of the believer's victory. We do not overcome the world by spiritual heroism; we overcome it by trusting the one who already has.

Assurance as Gift. The stated purpose of the letter — "that you may know that you have eternal life" (5:13) — stands as a rebuke to every theology that treats Christian assurance as presumption or spiritual pride. John writes to produce certainty. Reformed theology has always distinguished between assurance and presumption: presumption claims safety without evidence; assurance rests on the testimony of the Spirit, the evidence of new birth, and the promises of God. The three tests of the letter are not meant to produce anxiety but confirmation — the gentle hand of a faithful pastor showing the believer where the signs of life are visible. To know that you have eternal life is not arrogance; it is the appropriate response to the faithfulness of the God who cannot lie.
5.examples:
Then: The community, battered by false teaching and painful departure, needed to know one thing above all: that they had not missed it, that they were in the Son, that the life they had received was real and was eternal. John writes to give them that certainty — not a new experience, not a higher spirituality, but the settled confidence of those who have the Son and therefore have life. The simplicity of the final verdict — "whoever has the Son has life" — is both the most inclusive and most exclusive statement possible: inclusive, because anyone may have the Son; exclusive, because there is no life outside of him.

Now: In an age of therapeutic Christianity, where the goal is often feeling good about ourselves, John's letter is a corrective and a comfort. Assurance in John is not a feeling to be cultivated; it is a knowledge to be received — grounded in the testimony of God himself (5:9–10), confirmed by the evidence of new birth, and resting ultimately on the person of the Son. "This is the true God and eternal life" — Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, today, and forever. Whatever else may be uncertain in a Christian life, this is not: whoever has the Son has life, and the Son cannot be taken away.
